[1] The company cited the collapse of chum markets and a flood of low-priced Russian pink salmon as the primary reasons for this move. [1] An exception was made for coho fisheries in Petersburg and Cordova Sound to maintain support for those areas. [1] Trident's CEO, Joe Bundrant, and Senior Vice President, Jeff Welbourn, noted in the letter that Russia had recently harvested a volume of pink salmon equivalent to the entire annual forecast for Alaska and was selling it at very low prices, partly to fund the war in Ukraine. [3, 6] This news came as an additional blow to Alaskan fishermen who were already dealing with disappointingly low prices for Bristol Bay sockeye salmon, which had been set at a minimum of $0.50 per pound, a considerable decrease from the previous year's prices. [8] Trident attributed the market collapse to several factors, including a surge in Russian pink salmon harvests, which flooded the global market and drove down prices for all salmon species. [1, 3, 4] The devaluation of the Russian currency further exacerbated the situation, making their salmon exports cheaper and increasing competition for Alaskan fisheries. [3, 6] The plan allocates up to $67.5 million for sockeye salmon products, including $37.5 million for canned and $30 million for frozen fillets, and up to $52 million for Pacific groundfish, such as pollock, whiting, rockfish, and pink shrimp. [2, 5, 6] The governmental purchase was viewed by the industry as a significant form of inventory relief, intended to help stabilize the market ahead of the new 2023 fishing season. [1, 6] <9> In the weeks leading up to March 23, 2023, market suppliers reported a softening of US farmed salmon prices. Specifically, D-Trim fillets delivered to the Miami market were priced between $6.70 and $7.10 per pound. [2] It was anticipated that the seasonally strong demand for the upcoming Easter holiday would cause prices to rise again in the following weeks. [2] <10> During a panel at the National Fisheries Institute Global Seafood Market Conference, which ran from January 15 to 19, 2023, market data firm Kontali projected that the global supply of farmed Atlantic salmon would see a modest increase of approximately 1% in 2023. The forecast detailed a 3% production increase in Norway, which would be partially offset by an expected 2% decrease in Chile's production. This information was reported by news outlets on January 19, 2023.

[3] The price increase was attributed to a combination of a shortage of available fish and strong, demand-driven market pull from Asia, Europe, and the United States. [3] One farmer noted that prices for some weight classes were expected to reach NOK 93-97, with fish over 6 kg fetching over NOK 100 in the Chinese market. [3] While one exporter felt prices were becoming too high, another market participant highlighted the strong demand, predicting a robust market for May and June. [3] <2> In the first quarter of 2025, Norwegian salmon exports to the United States increased by 56% in volume compared to the same period in 2024, with 22,183 tonnes exported. This surge made the U.S. the largest single market for Norwegian salmon. The growth occurred as the market anticipated new U.S. import tariffs; a 15% tariff on Norwegian seafood was subsequently announced. Overall, Norway's seafood exports reached a record NOK 44 billion in the first quarter, with the U.S. being the fastest-growing market. <3> A market analysis report forecasts that the North American salmon market, valued at approximately USD 7.15 billion to USD 7.2 billion in 2024, is projected to grow, with one estimate predicting it will reach USD 7.48 billion in 2025. [3, 4] Forecasts for long-term growth vary, with projections estimating the market could reach between USD 10.78 billion and USD 11.5 billion by 2033. [3, 4] However, other market analyses present different valuations, with one report suggesting a market size of USD 6.22 billion in 2024 and another a significantly higher USD 13.46 billion. [2, 7] The United States is consistently identified as the dominant market in the region, accounting for a 75.4% share in 2024. [4] The fresh salmon segment is expected to experience the most rapid growth, with a predicted compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.7% for the period of 2025 to 2033. [4] <4> A market outlook for the U.S. seafood sector, published on February 21, 2025, anticipated mild growth in the first two quarters of the year, particularly in the fresh and frozen seafood segments. The report noted that while overall seafood prices had declined by 0.7% to 3.9%, making them more competitive with other proteins, a high average unit price of $9.57 could still limit consumer spending. <5> A forecast for the U.S. fish and seafood market indicates a projected revenue of $31.52 billion in 2025, with an anticipated annual growth rate of 3.10% from 2025 to 2029. A significant factor influencing market stability and pricing is the potential for tariffs on imported seafood, which accounts for nearly 94% of seafood consumed in the U.S. Other market analyses present varying figures; one projects the market to be valued at $30.1 billion in 2025 with a 4.8% CAGR through 2032, while another estimates the market at $24.7 billion in 2025 with a 1.29% CAGR to 2030. A separate forecast estimates the market at $56.93 billion in 2025 with a 3.1% CAGR until 2032. These different projections highlight the dynamic nature of the market and the various factors influencing its growth. <6> On January 15, 2025, seafood industry data provider Kontali published a market report analyzing end-of-year trade data from 2024 to offer insights into potential trends for early 2025. The report highlighted a 6% decline in Chilean Atlantic salmon exports to the US market in November 2024 compared to the previous year. This was part of a broader shift in supply dynamics, as the data also revealed a 30% decrease in exports to the EU, alongside a significant 73% increase to Russian markets. <7> In December 2024, U.S. retail seafood sales experienced a notable decline, contrary to typical holiday season trends. Total fresh seafood sales dropped by 5.4% in value to $738 million and 8.2% in volume compared to December 2023. This downturn was largely driven by a significant 12.6% decrease in fresh shellfish sales. In contrast to the overall negative trend, fresh salmon sales showed resilience with a modest increase of 0.5% in both value and volume. Other species like trout and cod also saw increases in sales. Frozen seafood sales also fell by 4.4% in value and 1.9% in volume. <8> U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo issued a determination of a fishery resource disaster for both the Sacramento River Fall Chinook and Klamath River Fall Chinook salmon fisheries in California for the 2024 season. [3, 4] The determination, announced on December 31, 2024, followed an April 11, 2024, request from California Governor Gavin Newsom and Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis. [3, 5, 13] This request was prompted by a unanimous recommendation from the Pacific Fishery Management Council to close California's commercial and recreational ocean salmon fishing season for the second consecutive year due to critically low salmon population forecasts. [5, 6, 14] The collapse of the iconic fisheries has been attributed to a combination of factors, including prolonged and historic drought, severe wildfires, impacts to spawning and rearing habitat, and extreme climate disruption. [4, 9, 12] The disaster declaration makes affected fishing communities eligible to seek federal financial relief, although the specific amount of assistance has not been determined. [4, 9] <9> Chilean salmon farming company Multi X reported a significant decrease in revenue for the third quarter of 2024, which concluded on September 30, 2024. The company attributed the drop to a combination of low average harvest weights and weak market prices. In the United States, its primary market, the average sales price fell to $5.49 per pound, a decrease from $5.73 per pound during the same period in 2023. This price decline was driven by weak consumer demand as customers opted for cheaper protein alternatives. <10> The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) released preliminary figures for the 2024 commercial salmon season, indicating significant declines in both harvest and value. The total catch was just over 101 million salmon, a 56% decrease from the 232 million fish caught in 2023. Fishermen collectively earned $304 million, which is nearly a 24% drop from the $398 million value recorded in the previous year. The preliminary report detailed the average ex-vessel (dockside) prices per pound for various salmon species: Sockeye at $1.05, Pink at $0.23, Chum at $0.39, Coho at $1.17, and Chinook at $5.11.
